basics: The perineum is the diamond-shaped floor of the trunk between the thighs, seen from below with the legs apart. Its corners are the pubic symphysis in front, the two ischial tuberosities (the bones you sit on) at the sides and the coccyx behind. A line between the ischial tuberosities cuts the diamond into two triangles: the front urogenital triangle carries the external genitals and urethral opening (penis and scrotum in a male), the rear anal triangle carries the anus. The scrotum is a pouch of loose skin and smooth muscle hanging from the root of the penis; it holds the testes, the epididymis on the back of each testis and the start of the ductus (vas) deferens. The testes hang outside for thermal reasons: sperm production needs about 2–3 °C below core temperature, and the cremaster and dartos muscles raise or lower them to regulate it. The same diamond exists in females.

terms.d: The diamond-shaped region between the thighs, from pubic symphysis to coccyx, containing the external genitals and anus.

basics: This is a front view with the skin of the scrotum and the lower abdominal wall cut away. Each testis sits in its own compartment; behind it lies the epididymis, from which the ductus deferens climbs upward inside the spermatic cord. The cord is a bundle: ductus deferens, testicular artery, a cooling plexus of veins, lymphatics, autonomic nerves and thin bands of skeletal muscle (the cremaster), wrapped in fascia. The cord leaves the scrotum and passes obliquely through the abdominal wall in the inguinal canal, entering at the superficial ring (what the slide labels) and emerging at the deep ring inside the abdomen; this is the route the testes took when they descended in the seventh fetal month. The penis in cross-section shows three erectile cylinders: two corpora cavernosa above and the corpus spongiosum below carrying the spongy (penile) urethra, the single tube serving both urination and ejaculation.

basics: A testis is an oval gland about 5 cm long. Its white fibrous capsule (tunica albuginea) sends walls inward that divide it into 200–300 wedge-shaped lobules, each packed with one to three tightly coiled seminiferous tubules; the right-hand photo shows their cut ends. These tubules are the sperm factory. From them, sperm pass through straight tubules into a network (rete testis), then through efferent ductules into the single, hugely coiled duct of the epididymis, the comma-shaped structure on the back of the testis: an upper head, a body and a lower tail that becomes the ductus deferens. Sperm leaving the tubules are complete in shape but cannot yet swim; during roughly two weeks in the epididymis they gain motility and fertilising ability, and can be stored there for months. The spermatic cord at the top is the bundle of duct, vessels and nerves leaving the scrotum. The slide leaves the duct sequence and the capsule unnamed.

basics: Every body cell carries 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs (diploid, 2n). A gamete must carry only one of each pair (haploid, n) so that fertilisation restores 46; meiosis is the two-step division that halves the number. Read the figure from the outside of the tubule wall inward. Spermatogonia at the basement membrane divide by ordinary mitosis, keeping a permanent stem-cell reserve. A cell that moves inward becomes a primary spermatocyte, copies its DNA (each chromosome now two chromatids), and in meiosis I the homologous pairs line up, swap segments (crossing-over) and are pulled apart, giving two secondary spermatocytes with 23 double-stranded chromosomes. Meiosis II separates the chromatids, giving four spermatids. Spermiogenesis is remodelling, not division: the round spermatid grows an acrosome cap and a tail, packs mitochondria into a midpiece and sheds spare cytoplasm (eaten by nurse cells). Daughter cells stay linked by cytoplasmic bridges, so a patch of tubule matures in step.

refs.section_title: Autosomes, Sex Chromosomes, and Sex Determination
refs.capture: p.1194 right column: the two paragraphs under the heading 'Autosomes, Sex Chromosomes, and Sex Determination' (start 'When viewed under a microscope'): 22 pairs of autosomes plus XX or XY; meiosis gives two X-sperm and two Y-sperm; p.1195 left column top: Figure 29.25 'Sex determination' (Punnett square) — explains the slide's '22X or 22Y'.

basics: A sperm is a stripped-down delivery vehicle for 23 chromosomes, about 60 µm long, most of it tail. The flattened head holds the condensed nucleus capped by the acrosome, a bag of enzymes (hyaluronidase, proteases) that later digests a path through the coats around the oocyte. Behind it the neck holds the centrioles that built the tail's microtubules; the middle piece is wrapped in spiral mitochondria that make ATP for swimming; the principal piece is the long whip and the end piece its taper. '22X or 22Y' means 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome: half of all sperm carry X and half Y, so the sperm decides the baby's sex. The right-hand column is the cell lineage: a diploid stem cell (spermatogonium) becomes a primary spermatocyte, meiosis I gives two secondary spermatocytes (23 chromosomes each), meiosis II four spermatids, and spermiogenesis then reshapes each spermatid into the sperm drawn on the left. Ejaculated sperm survive about 48 hours.

basics: A hormone is a chemical released into the blood that acts on distant cells carrying its receptor. The testis is run by a three-level chain. Neurons in the hypothalamus release gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) into a short portal blood system feeding the anterior pituitary, whose gonadotroph cells respond by releasing two gonadotropins, LH and FSH, into the general circulation. In the testis, LH acts on the interstitial (Leydig) cells between the tubules, which make testosterone from cholesterol; being a steroid, it diffuses out into blood. FSH acts on the nurse (Sertoli) cells inside the tubules, which, with testosterone, support spermatogenesis and secrete androgen-binding protein that keeps local testosterone high. The system is self-limiting like a thermostat: rising testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH, and nurse cells release inhibin, which suppresses FSH once sperm output is sufficient. The slide leaves out nurse cells, inhibin, the feedback loops and the fact that FSH acts indirectly; the end product is sperm, not 'spermatocytes'.

basics: The picture is a midline (sagittal) cut through the pelvis, face to the right. Follow the numbers as a plumbing diagram. (1) The ductus (vas) deferens, a 45 cm muscular tube, leaves the tail of the epididymis, rises in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal into the pelvis, hooks over the ureter and runs down the back of the bladder, widening into an ampulla. (2) Beside it lies the seminal vesicle (seminal gland), a coiled pouch that adds most of the seminal fluid. At ejaculation the duct's three smooth-muscle layers contract in waves under sympathetic control. The slide does not say the urethra is shared with the urinary system or name its three parts.

basics: Now the same plumbing is seen from behind, with the bladder above. The two ductus deferentia come down the back of the bladder and their ampullae lie medial to the two seminal vesicles; each pair joins into an ejaculatory duct that enters the prostate from above and opens into the prostatic urethra. Below the prostate the urethra passes through the sheet of deep perineal muscles (the slide's 'perineal membrane') as the short membranous urethra, and then runs the length of the corpus spongiosum as the spongy urethra. The pea-sized bulbourethral glands sit in that muscle sheet beside the membranous urethra and drain into the spongy urethra. So the full path from testis to exterior is: seminiferous tubule → straight tubules → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis → ductus deferens → ejaculatory duct → prostatic, membranous and spongy urethra. Along the way the three gland types add the fluid that makes up most of semen.

basics: This is a coronal (frontal) section: the penis is cut in the plane of its width and opened like a book. At the top the bladder empties into the prostatic urethra, encircled by the prostate; the urethra then squeezes through the perineal muscle sheet (membranous part) and enters the penis, running to the tip inside the corpus spongiosum (spongy part). The shaft is three parallel cylinders of erectile tissue, each in a tough fibrous sleeve: the paired corpora cavernosa (the striped bodies on the slide) above, and the single corpus spongiosum below, which swells at the end into the glans. Erectile tissue is a sponge of blood-filled spaces walled by smooth muscle. During arousal, parasympathetic nerves release nitric oxide; the supplying arterioles and sinus walls relax, blood pours in, the swelling squashes the draining veins, and the organ stiffens. Ejaculation, by contrast, is a sympathetic reflex. The slide's names are misspelt (see note).

basics: Semen is sperm suspended in seminal fluid, and the fluid comes from four sources, not two: a little from the seminiferous tubules, about 60 % from the seminal glands, about 25 % from the prostate, and a small mucous contribution from the bulbourethral glands. Seminal-gland fluid is alkaline and viscous and carries fructose as fuel, prostaglandins that stir the female tract, and proteins that make the ejaculate clot briefly. Prostatic fluid is milky and slightly acidic, with citric acid, an antibiotic peptide, and enzymes (including PSA) that liquefy the clot after 10–20 minutes. The net pH of 7.2–7.7 protects sperm from the acid of the urethra and vagina. A typical ejaculate is 2.5–5 mL holding 50–150 million sperm per mL; below 20 million/mL fertility falls, because only a few hundred of the millions ever reach the oocyte. Sperm become fully fertile only after capacitation inside the female tract. The slide's '(spermatocytes/spermatids)' is loose: semen contains sperm.

basics: The graph plots four blood hormone levels against the cycle day. (1) FSH from the anterior pituitary rises slightly at the start and recruits a group of follicles. basics: Oogenesis uses the same meiosis as sperm production but on a very different schedule and with a lopsided division. Before birth, oogonia multiply by mitosis, most die, and the survivors become primary oocytes that begin meiosis I and then freeze in its first stage (prophase I). They stay frozen through childhood, so an oocyte ovulated at 40 has waited 40 years. From puberty, each month one primary oocyte in a maturing follicle completes meiosis I, but the cytoplasm is split unequally: almost all goes to the secondary oocyte, the rest to a tiny discarded first polar body. The secondary oocyte freezes again in metaphase II and is ovulated in that state. Only if a sperm enters does it finish meiosis II, shedding a second polar body and becoming an ovum whose nucleus fuses with the sperm's to form the diploid zygote. Net yield: one ovum per primary oocyte (plus polar bodies that die), versus four sperm per primary spermatocyte.

basics: The ovulated secondary oocyte is wrapped in two coats: an outer cloud of granulosa cells (corona radiata) and a clear glycoprotein shell (zona pellucida). A capacitated sperm wriggles between the corona cells; binding to a zona protein (ZP3) bursts its acrosome, and the released enzymes plus tail thrust dig a channel through the zona. The first sperm to touch the oocyte's membrane fuses with it; within seconds the membrane depolarises (fast block) and calcium-triggered secretions harden the zona (slow block), so no second sperm can enter. Entry restarts the frozen meiosis II: it finishes, casting off a second polar body, and the cell is now an ovum. Sperm and egg nuclei swell into pronuclei, migrate together and fuse (syngamy), restoring 46 chromosomes: the zygote. The arithmetic at the bottom: every ovum carries 22 autosomes + X; a sperm carries 22 + X or 22 + Y; the zygote is 44 + XX (female) or 44 + XY (male).

basics: After ovulation the corpus luteum is programmed to die in two weeks, and its death is what triggers menstruation. An embryo prevents this with a hormonal message: from about day 8 its outer cell layer (trophoblast, later the chorion) secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a molecule that mimics LH. hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive and secreting progesterone and estrogens, so the endometrium is retained and the expected period never comes; hCG in urine is what pregnancy tests detect. On the graph hCG (red) climbs steeply to a peak around week 9 and then falls away. Meanwhile the chorion, and from about week 12 the fully formed placenta, takes over making estrogens and progesterone directly, and these (green and brown) rise steadily until birth. Progesterone keeps the uterine muscle relaxed and the cervix shut; estrogens drive uterine and breast growth. The placenta also makes relaxin, hCS and CRH, which the slide omits.

basics: Once fertilised in the ampulla, the zygote is carried toward the uterus by the tube's cilia and peristalsis while dividing by mitosis without growing (cleavage): two cells at about 30 hours, four on day 2, a solid 16-cell ball (morula) by day 3–4, still inside the zona pellucida and no bigger than the original egg. Entering the uterus on day 4–5 it absorbs endometrial secretions, a fluid cavity opens inside, and it becomes a blastocyst: an inner cell mass (embryoblast) that will form the embryo and an outer shell (trophoblast) that will form the placenta and chorion. It hatches from the zona, floats for two days, and around day 6 sticks to the secretory-phase endometrium; by day 7 trophoblast enzymes have burrowed it in and it starts secreting hCG. All times count from fertilisation. An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, usually in a tube narrowed by scarring; the tube cannot expand, and rupture with internal bleeding is life-threatening.

basics: The embryonic period is fertilisation to the end of week 8: every organ system is laid down, so this is when drugs, radiation and infections do most harm. By week 8 the embryo has a human face, separate fingers and toes and the limb regions named on the drawing; the liver bulges because it is then the main blood-forming organ. From week 9 to birth it is a fetus: mainly growth and maturation. Birth comes about 38 weeks after fertilisation; clinicians count 40 weeks from the last menstrual period, the slide's figure. The placenta is a disc built by both individuals: fetal chorionic villi dipping into pools of maternal blood in the endometrium. The bloodstreams never mix; oxygen and nutrients diffuse across the villus wall one way, wastes the other. The umbilical cord links them: two arteries carry low-oxygen fetal blood to the placenta, one vein brings oxygenated blood back, sheathed in shiny amnion, the surface in the photo.
